narrative: The model estimated a 47% chance that you will leave. That is not a certainty, but in this promotion process it is treated as a meaningful departure risk, which is why the promotion was denied. The strongest influence was your total experience of one to five years. This is common among employees predicted to stay—about half have that level—so it pulled the estimate toward staying. The next strongest signal was that you reported other job opportunities. Most employees predicted to stay reported none, so this pushed the estimate toward leaving. The third signal was training in the last three years: you attended one to three programs, a level that was slightly more associated with leaving than having no training, so it also nudged the risk upward. Overall, your experience profile is stabilizing, but outside opportunities and the training pattern raise concern. Before reapplying, you should discuss career progression and internal mobility with your manager, clarify promotion criteria, and ask how your training can be applied to a visible growth path. The organization should also check whether your access to opportunities, recognition, and development is being managed fairly, because retaining you may depend on addressing those concerns directly.
